title: Working on Drywall Stilts
summary: Stilts put your feet higher and make every trip hazard on the floor more dangerous. This talk covers what OSHA's scaffold rules require when stilts are used, plus the floor and lighting conditions that keep you upright.
talking_points: Stilts must be properly maintained, and any change to the original equipment must be approved by the manufacturer (29 CFR 1926.452(y)(4)).
The surface you walk on in stilts must be flat and free of pits, holes and obstructions such as debris, and free of other tripping and falling hazards (1926.452(y)(3)).

Walk the whole area before you strap in. Scrap, cords, screws and boards left on the floor are exactly the debris this rule is talking about. Debris must be kept cleared from work areas, passageways and stairs (1926.25(a)).
An employee may wear stilts on a scaffold only if it is a large area scaffold (1926.452(y)(1)). Do not walk up to a mobile tower or a small platform on stilts.
Where a guardrail system provides fall protection on a large area scaffold, the guardrail must be raised by the height of the stilts being used (1926.452(y)(2)).

Light matters. Construction areas, corridors and storage areas must be lit to at least the minimum levels in Table D-3 while work is in progress, for example 5 foot-candles for general construction area lighting and for indoor corridors and hallways (1926.56(a)). If you cannot see the floor ahead of you, stop and get more light.
site_hazards_to_check: Screws, cords, joint compound buckets or scrap boards on the floor
Holes, floor openings, gaps or uneven slab transitions
Stilts that are damaged, loose or modified from the original
Dim work areas or shadows across the floor
Guardrails on a large area scaffold not raised to account for stilt height
discussion_questions: Who walks the floor before stilts go on, and what do we do with what we find?
Has anyone altered or repaired their stilts, and was it approved by the manufacturer?
Where on this job is the floor not flat or not clear enough for stilts?
